narrative:
Based on the information in your application, the model estimated a 50% chance that you would be a bad credit risk. That is not a low-risk result—it means your profile does not show enough signs of reliability, and as a result your loan application was denied.

The strongest factor working against you was your checking account. Your account is currently overdrawn, with a balance below zero. Among approved applicants, only about 12.6% had such an account; most had a positive balance or no overdraft at all. This is a major red flag because it suggests you may already be struggling to manage your finances, before taking on a new loan.

The second most important factor was the length of the loan you requested. Here, the news is better: you asked for a 12-month term, which is shorter than the average approved loan of about 19 months. A shorter repayment period usually means less time for something to go wrong, so the model viewed this as a positive factor. Unfortunately, it was not enough to outweigh the checking account concern.

The third factor was the purpose of the loan. You requested the money to buy a new car. Loans for new cars made up only about 16.5% of approved applications and this type of purchase was associated with higher risk. New cars lose value quickly and the loan amount is often larger, which may have pushed the model further toward denying you.

To improve your chances in the future, focus first on restoring a positive balance in your checking account and keeping it stable for several months. Consider applying for a smaller loan, or for a different purpose, and wait until your overall financial situation looks stronger. Reapplying soon with the same profile would likely lead to the same result.
